fig7_1: Four-panel comparison of node distributions on the interval minus one to one for sixteen intervals. The top panel shows equispaced points spread uniformly along the line; the middle panel shows Chebyshev-Gauss-Lobatto points bunched tightly near both endpoints and sparse in the centre. The bottom-left panel draws a semicircle with equally spaced points around its arc dropping vertical projections down to the axis, illustrating that Chebyshev nodes are these projections. The bottom-right panel compares spacing near the left boundary, showing Chebyshev gaps shrinking like one over N squared versus the uniform one over N gaps of the equispaced grid.
fig7_2: Two-panel view of the sixteen-by-sixteen Chebyshev differentiation matrix. The left panel is a heatmap of the matrix entries with red for positive and blue for negative values, dominated by the two large opposite-sign corner entries at the top-left and bottom-right; the off-diagonal pattern shows alternating signs. The right panel overlays two row profiles versus column index: the boundary row in red towers far above the interior row in green, whose entries are too small to discern at this shared scale, dramatizing the order N squared size of the corner values.
fig7_3: Line-and-marker profile of a single interior row, row nine, of the sixteen-by-sixteen Chebyshev differentiation matrix, plotting entry value against column index. The curve oscillates with alternating positive and negative signs, the largest magnitude at the diagonal column nine, with smaller but non-negligible spikes persisting at the boundary columns zero and sixteen, illustrating the global reach of spectral differentiation and stencil-like sign alternation at far smaller magnitude than a boundary row.
fig7_4: Two panels illustrating Chebyshev cardinal (Lagrange basis) functions. The left panel overlays several smooth polynomial curves for ten intervals, each rising to exactly one at its own node and crossing zero at every other node, with oscillations between nodes. The right panel isolates one cardinal function and draws short tangent line segments at each grid point; the caption notes these tangent slopes equal the entries of the matching column of the differentiation matrix.
fig7_5: Grid of panels demonstrating Chebyshev spectral differentiation of the Witch of Agnesi, one over one plus four x squared, for ten and twenty grid points. The top row plots the bell-shaped function values sampled at the clustered Chebyshev points. The bottom row overlays the exact derivative curve with the spectral approximation, which sits essentially on top of it, annotated with the maximum error; the error shrinks sharply from ten to twenty points, confirming exponential convergence.
tbl7_1: Table listing the maximum Chebyshev differentiation error for the Witch of Agnesi at grid sizes from four up to fifty, showing the error falling from order one tenth to about six times ten to the power minus nine, demonstrating exponential decay with N.
fig7_6: Four log-scale convergence plots of maximum differentiation error versus the number of points N, one per test function, with the vertical error axis logarithmic. Top left, the function absolute value of x to the five-halves power follows a straight algebraic descent of slope about minus two and a half set by its limited Holder smoothness. Top right, the bump function e to the power minus one over one minus x squared falls faster than any straight power-law line yet does not reach the exponential straight line, the super-algebraic regime. Bottom left, hyperbolic tangent of five x descends as a straight line on the semilog axes down to machine precision, the geometric analytic regime. Bottom right, the polynomial x to the eighth drops abruptly to round-off and stays flat once N reaches eight, being differentiated exactly.
